title: James Zou - Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science

segments.text: [APPLAUSE]
SPEAKER 1: [INAUDIBLE]
JAMES ZOU: All right.
Thank you very much.
I'm really excited to participate here.
So I lead the AI for Science lab at Stanford.
And one of the ideas that I'm really excited about recently
is thinking about, how do we try to scale the number of agents,
the number of AI scientists agents
that actually collaborate and work together?
So I think that's actually a really exciting new direction
of scaling.
So instead of scaling individual models,
but scaling the number of agents,
from tens of agents to hundreds, to thousands, and even millions
of agents that collaborate, and see what
are the new kinds of capabilities that emerges.
So I want to give some examples of that kinds
of agentic scaling.
So the first step we took in this direction
is, we created this virtual lab, which has initially,
a team of 5 to 10 agents that emulate
my physical lab at Stanford.
So in the virtual lab, we have an AI professor agent
that runs the lab.
And then working with the professor,
we have a bunch of different AI students
with different expertise, ranging from mathematics to data
science to protein design.
And the agents have their own group meetings.
We give them a budget, so they can actually
run some experiments.
We also created, for the agents, a replica of Stanford agent
school, where they can go to the school
to become better researchers in their specific domains.
And after we created this virtual lab,
we give the agents several different tasks.
So here it is in this demo, I'll show you
the first project we assigned to the agents, which actually help
us to design good binders to some of the recent SARS-CoV
variants.
So in this demo, this illustrates
one of the agent group meetings, where the professor first
explains to the student agents what is
the goal here of the project.
And then the different agents, different experts
then can speak up and contribute their ideas.
In this case, the immunologists recommended
designing a nanobody.
And then the machine learning agent
then came up with some ideas, how
to optimize these nanobodies.
So after a series of these agent group meetings
and one-on-one discussions between the agents,
they actually designed a pretty interesting
computational framework for optimizing
these nanobody proteins, which is different from what
people have published before.
And then by running that framework,
then they came back to us with a few of these new nanobodies
that they designed.
And then we, with our experimental collaborators,
then we synthesized these proteins.
And we tested them in the real world,
to show they were actually quite effective binders.
In particular, they were actually better binders
than the best previous human designed nanobodies
to some of the recent COVID variants.
So this, to us, was actually quite an exciting first step
to illustrate how a team of agents, when they collaborate,
can actually solve these quite challenging, open-ended projects
that we can then experimentally validate.
So for our next step, we want to be even more ambitious.
So we said, OK, so can we actually now
have tried to emulate a much more complex organization
of an entire pharma company now with tens of thousands
of AI scientists agents.
So we call this the virtual biotech.
So in the virtual biotech, we have a CSO agent,
the Chief Scientist Officer agent that
runs the virtual biotech with its own chief of staff,
its own office, and lawyers, and so on.
And then under the CSO agent are these different divisions
that mirrors the standard divisions you see
in the human pharma company.
For example, we have a division of agents
that looks for good targets, another division that designs
the molecules given those targets, a third one that
designs clinical trials and looks at safety and so on.
And all of these divisions now are operationalized
by different AI scientist agents with different roles
and specializations.
For example, under the target identification division,
there's one agent that's really good at looking
at all the genetics data under the agent that's
really good at doing single cell analysis and so on.
And all of these agents then can collaborate and tackle
these much harder problems.
So here's one example of the project we
assigned to this virtual biotech now,
which is to help us design new therapeutics
for a particular target in lung cancer,
called CD276, which is a transmembrane protein that
has the effect of suppressing immune response.
So a lot of pharma companies are interested in this target.
So we said, OK, can the virtual biotech
actually help us to design a new therapeutic for this target?
And then this team of agents involving many thousands
of agents, then they actually did
a lot of comprehensive analysis, looking
at both genetic data, genomics data, patients data, and so on.
And by analyzing these disease mechanisms,
then they came back to us with actually,
a specific design, what's called ADC, or Antibody Drug Conjugate,
where you have an antibody that's
actually designed for this specific CD276 protein.
And then antibodies that are linked to a warhead, which they
got chemotherapy payload, which then is released
when antibody hits that target.
So this is actually quite a relatively new design.
And we haven't seen this before for CD276.
And then what's really exciting was that several months later,
so Merck, a large company, then independently actually designed
the same antibody drug conjugate for CD276.
And then they experimentally tested this in human populations
to show that it's actually quite effective,
which received FDA breakthrough designation.
So this, to us, was also really exciting,
as a way to independently see how
the designs from our virtual biotech
can then be independently corroborated
by human studies, in this case, from Merck.
In order to design and make all these thousands of agents work
effectively in science, we found that that's actually
really useful to actually create a new layer of infrastructures
and environments for these scientists agents.
So for example, a lot of the existing scientific databases,
including databases that contains
all of these biological proteins,
they're mostly designed to be consumed by humans, also
consumed by pre-AI algorithms.
So often, these databases and APIs
are too brittle and too limited to be
used by agents efficiently.
So what we did was to actually then
take all these existing databases that contains millions
of proteins, and molecules, and gene expressions,
and then convert all of that into agent-native virtual file
systems, which makes it much easier for AI scientists agents
and to be able to synthesize and then
aggregate information across all of these different data sources.
And here's just a comparison that shows
what we call this paper clip.
And then here's a comparison that
shows that if you actually use this agent-native virtual file
systems to represent all of the scientific data
sets and knowledge, so you actually
get much better accuracy compared to, let's say,
if you use cloud science or the latest cloud models.
But it's also an order of magnitude faster and cheaper
than if you give the same language models
access to these databases through these traditional MCPs
or APIs.
So we've actually gone through this process of essentially,
using this virtual file systems now
to identify all of scientific knowledge, which includes all
of the papers that people have published,
full text papers on the archive and other places,
and all these different databases that's all actually
under paper clip.
It's all free, actually, so you can then, with one line of code,
then give all of that knowledge to your agents
in this virtual file system that enables agents to be much more
effective in leveraging this.
So this is one of the infrastructures
that we built that enables the virtual biotech
to be much more effective.
So the last part I want to mention
is now, we talk about how we can go from a virtual lab with tens
of agents to a virtual biotech now with tens of thousands
of agents.
But what happens?
Can we scale that even further, where
we have millions of scientists agents that collaborate?
So I think this is a really exciting opportunity for us
to really reimagine what OAuth human knowledge would
look like when we try to identify them.
So the past hundreds of years, the way that humans represent
knowledge is really in the form of these very passive artifacts
that we call static papers.
So the people will write this paper.
But often, it's very difficult for readers or for collaborators
to figure out how to adapt the knowledge from that paper
just by reading the static words.
So our idea is that, why don't we
turn all of those static artifacts of knowledge
from papers into dynamic and interactive virtual authors
that we call paper agents?
So each paper agent then is like a virtual author
that represents all the knowledge from that paper.
So in this case, so here, I can just ask the paper agent,
can you help me to apply the method from that paper
to my own data sets to my own problem?
And the paper agent then will do that automatically and generate
reproducible workflows, and come back to me
with the end discoveries and results.
So the goal of this is that by identifying
all of these passive knowledge into dynamic virtual authors,
then this makes knowledge much easier to disseminate,
also easier to form collaborations.
So under the hood, we created actually this paper
to agent automated workflow that converts static knowledge
into dynamic agents.
So briefly, what happens is that we
have a bunch of different worker agents
that goes into the original paper and any associated
code and data.
And these worker agents basically
creates a virtual environment, trying
to replicate the original research process, for example,
by replicating the results from that paper.
In the process of doing that, then we actually
create this paper agent or the paper MCP,
which then can be turned into a paper agent.
So one of the applications of this
is that now, we can actually ask the knowledge agents to help
to make sure that knowledge itself is actually reproducible.
So in this case, the paper agent is
able to generate all the intermediate figures and results
that matches the original publication.
So in this case, the paper was reproducible.
But in many other cases, it also found that the paper agent
actually identified key mistakes and limitations
in the original publications.
So the last part, the thing I'll mention
is that, I think maybe the most exciting application of all
of these paper agents is that I think
this enables a new form of collaborations
between different agents.
So we're now in the process of identifying
every paper that people have ever published.
So that will create actually, millions of paper agents.
And now, these agents are starting to talk to each other
to generate new collaborations.
So this is a real example of this,
where Google DeepMind published a paper called AlphaGenome
a few months ago.
So it's paper to agent that was identified into an agent that
knows how to use that tool.
And then a separate research group
published a genetic data set for mutations linked
to GWAS for risk for ADHD that was also
turned into a paper agent that knows how to use that data set.
In this case, those two agents actually started
to talk to each other, decided they could collaborate,
and then automatically discover a new mutation
that increases the risk for ADHD, which is not known before.
So we're starting to see many more
of these examples of these paper agents starting to collaborate.
So I'll wrap up here.
So I hope to show these few examples to illustrate why we're
really excited about this new axis of capabilities that
emerges when we're scaling up the number of scientist agents
that starts to collaborate, and work with each other,
and also work with human researchers.
Thank you very much.
[APPLAUSE]
